notes: What is the second creature described to illustrate God's strength? (41:1-34) - Leviathan, which some think may be the crocodile

quotes.text: God continued to question Job, turning next to an unknown monster "leviathan" (see Isa. 27:1 for a metaphorical use of this name; it may here refer to a crocodile). The questions reflect man's inability to communicate, negotiate, or play with such a beast. The questions point out man's incapacity to attack this creature or subdue it or even to stand at the sight of it, and part of the lesson is this: if man dare not stand before one of God's great creatures, who can stand before Him? (Job 41:1-10). The point is driven home with further details of all the marvelous body parts and capabilities of the beast.
quotes.speaker: Ellis T. Rasmussen
quotes.source: A Latter-day Saint Commentary on the Old Testament
quotes.attr: Ellis T. Rasmussen, A Latter-day Saint Commentary on the Old Testament, p.412

notes: What key point does God make with Leviathan? (41:10) - The animal is so fierce, none would dare stir him up; who then is able to stand against God?
Job 41:10 10 None [is so] fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?

quotes.text: Another terrifying aspect of the vision is the horses with their mouths filled with lion's teeth, the embodiment of cruelty and destruction, out of which issue fire, smoke, and brimstone, symbolic of the torment of hell and underscoring the diabolical nature of the horde. John's horses echo the monster Leviathan of Job 41:19-20, who breathes out fire and smoke. By this imagery, John shows that it is grounded in the very heart of Satan's domain.
quotes.speaker: Richard D. Draper
quotes.source: Opening the Seven Seals: The Visions of John the Revelator
quotes.attr: Richard D. Draper, Opening the Seven Seals: The Visions of John the Revelator, p.108
